Such a non-profit open source model still requires funding and resources to be put towards the development of the projects if they are to continue being successful. An example of such a project is the WarpX collaboration [23, 2, 9], based out of Berkeley Lab [5], discussed as a case study below. A common collaboration model for large entities is that used by technology transfer offices, where a number of license mechanisms can be used to move technology from the institution to outside parties. This mindset that the work performed at an institution should be monetized, rather than accepting a shared responsibility to community collaborations, is particularly challenging for AI/ML technologies, even within the specialized sphere of accelerator operations. We were unable to find any examples of academic- or government-led collaborations in AI/ML, likely due (at least in part) to these unhelpful points of view and associated contract mechanisms. We next consider three successful software collaborations in the particle accelerator community, so as to highlighthowtheseeffortshavegrownorbeendevelopedinthecurrentfundingandregulatoryenvironment. 15 4.1.1 Case Study: Xopt [10] Xopt is an optimization toolkit that is used at an increasing number of facilities to perform Bayesian op- timization for a variety of control needs, both operational and scientific. The tool is coupled with a GUI front end known as Badger [11]. xopt was originally developed by SLAC engineers and staff, in particular Dr. Christopher Mayes and Dr. Ryan Roussel. This project has been successful for a number of reasons, including: • Monetary and personnel support from a large facility (SLAC) • An enthusiastic advocate pushes for the tool’s use across multiple facilities (Dr. Roussel) • Sufficient generality to fill a need for multiple facilities across academia, industry, and government Xopt provides a toolkit that is of significant value to the accelerator operations community. The project leadership (i.e. specific individuals) provide strong support for Xopt users. The SLAC National Accelerator Lab [19] actively provides resources for the deployment and development of the tool in both travel and personnel funds, and the project leadership are strong evangelists for the software. Deployment and usage varies across different facilities. Several other Bayesian optimization toolkits are available and would likely have been deployed independently by different accelerator groups if Xopt did not provide these resources for communication and development support. 4.1.2 Case Study: WarpX [2, 23, 9] WarpX was initially developed at Berkeley Lab as a part of the Exascale Computing Project (ECP), with supportfrominternallabfunding, andhasgrowntoincludesupportfromEuropeanagencies, inadditionto other Department of Energy funding streams. Since the end of ECP funding, the governance and funding modelhaveshifted. Forexample,theprojecthasbecomeafoundingmemberoftheLinuxFoundation’sHigh Performance Software Foundation [12]. The Linux Foundation model is such that each project is classified as a Linux Foundation project. The WarpX collaboration has been successful due to its access to a number of funding sources from multiple funding offices, strong personalities leading the development who regularly reach out to users and partners, and multi-country interest in the success of the project leading to additional buy-in.
